//: The literal gate's configuration, read by tools/check-owner-literals.mjs. Two kinds of pattern:
the NEUTRAL ones below, which ship with the public repo and catch what no project should
publish (a private-network address, a home folder, a personal email address, a live key); and
an install owner's own names (domain, people, channel ids), which live in a separate file that
never ships — tools/owner-literals.json — and are added when that file is present. A tree that
has owner folders must have that file too, or the gate refuses to run.
Comments are COUNTED on purpose: a public reader sees them. Every pattern is matched
case-insensitively (unless it says caseSensitive) and counted per occurrence; a match listed in `allow` is not counted.

patterns.name: private-network address
patterns.why: an address inside someone's own network (RFC 1918, carrier-grade NAT): a real host on a contributor's LAN does not belong in public code

allow.^\\d{1,3}\\.\\d{1,3}\\.\\d{1,3}\\.0$: a network's own address, written as the start of a range (the backup-target blocklist names its ranges this way)
allow.^172\\.29\\.83\\.\\d{1,3}$: the bundle's own Docker network (install/compose.yaml, BB_SUBNET) — the same on every install
allow.^10\\.0\\.0\\.[1-9]$: the example LAN hosts tests and placeholders use (a self-hosted model server, a peer that is not trusted)
allow.^192\\.168\\.1\\.(?:1|20)$: example LAN hosts the SSRF and backup-target tests use
allow.^172\\.16\\.5\\.5$: an example host in the 172.16/12 range for the SSRF tests
allow.^172\\.17\\.0\\.1$: Docker's default bridge gateway, which the backup-target check refuses
allow.^100\\.64\\.0\\.1$|^100\\.127\\.255\\.25: the first and last host of carrier-grade NAT, for the backup-target tests
allow.^100\\.100\\.100\\.200$: a cloud provider's metadata address the backup-target check refuses

patterns.name: home folder path
patterns.why: a path inside one person's home folder — the code must not depend on where a contributor keeps it

allow.^/home/nonroot/$: the unprivileged user of distroless container images
allow.^/home/node/$: the unprivileged user of the official node image

patterns.name: personal email address
patterns.why: a person's real address; examples use a reserved domain (example.*, .test, .invalid, .arpa)

allow.@(?:[a-z0-9-]+\\.)*example(?:\\.[a-z]+)?: a reserved example domain (RFC 2606), or example.<any> by the same convention
allow.@paypal\\.com$: PayPal's own sender addresses, which its webhook payloads carry
allow.\\.service$: a systemd template unit (name@instance.service), not an address
allow.^git@: an ssh git remote, not an address

patterns.name: live payment key
patterns.why: a live Stripe secret or restricted key — tests use test-mode or obviously fake values

patterns.name: private key block
patterns.why: a private key — its header followed by key material; keys are generated on the box or in the test, never written into the tree (a test's placeholder body is not key material)

patterns.name: private IPv6 host address
patterns.why: a whole host address inside someone's own network (IPv6 unique-local fc00::/7, or link-local fe80::/10), written out or compressed (`::` anywhere) — the IPv6 twin of the private-network address; a range (fc00::/7, fd12:3456::/64) has no host part and is not one

allow.^fe80::1$: the link-local example the address guards and their tests name (the SSRF guard, the backup-target check)
allow.^fc00::[15]$: unique-local examples the address guards and their tests name
allow.^fd12:3456::1$: a unique-local example the backup-target tests name
allow.^fd00:ec2::254$: a cloud provider's IPv6 metadata address, which the backup-target check refuses

patterns.name: signed token
patterns.why: a signed JWT (header, claims, signature) — a session or API credential; tests build their own tokens at run time

patterns.name: chat webhook URL
patterns.why: a Discord or Slack webhook URL — the URL is the credential: whoever has it can post as the hook

ownerRoots.//: Exempt — the private build's home for owner-only code and content. The public cut drops these folders, so a literal inside one never ships. web's is the route group (owner): owner pages and API routes keep their URLs, and deleting the folder deletes them. tools/check-owner-seam.mjs reads this list too: product code reaches each folder only through its package's one seam file.

zeroPaths.//: Folders outside the packages that ship as they are and must hold NO literal at all — no baseline, no ratchet, zero. Checked on EVERY run of the scanner, whichever package it was pointed at, so no package script or CI line can forget them. No exclusion applies inside one: a README, a test or a comment here is published as it is. A path that does not exist is reported and passes. The whole public tree is checked the same way by `--tree` (every file, no exclusion).
zeroPaths.migrations/baseline/: the fresh-install baseline schema + seeds: the database every new install starts from
zeroPaths.install/: the installer and bundle: runs on every install's box
zeroPaths.config/: the shared definitions every package generates its copies from
zeroPaths.public-root/: the files the public cut places at the root of the public repo (README, SECURITY, CONTRIBUTING, .github)

notScanned.//: Exclusions for the per-package RATCHET only — `--tree` and the zero paths apply none of them. Every exclusion states its reason.

segments..next: web's build output — compiled copies of the source being scanned
segments.__fixtures__: recorded provider payloads (Stripe test mode, PayPal, feeds) — test data that must stay byte-for-byte what the provider sent

prefixes.stream-ingest/config/: the bot's persona files — install content, not code, and not part of the public cut. A prefix, not a segment: web/app/api/billing/paypal/config/ is code and IS scanned

files.\\.(test|probe)\\.[cm]?[jt]sx?$: tests: the ratchet counts product code; the whole public tree, tests included, is held at zero by `--tree`
files.\\.md$: documentation — held at zero in the public tree by `--tree`
